title: Billy the Kid: An Autobiography
author: Pat F. Garrett
edition_analyzed: Standard annotated edition, most widely referenced version
target_audience: Readers interested in the American Old West
Fans of true crime and outlaw stories
Scholars studying legend versus fact in American history
core_themes: Myth and reality of the outlaw figure
Law, justice, and morality in the frontier era
Construction of public image and legend
Survival, violence, and youth in the Wild West
primary_purpose: To recount the life and exploits of Billy the Kid from the perspective of Pat Garrett, the sheriff who ultimately killed him, and to serve as both a historical record and a means to set the record straight regarding Garrett’s role and the truth behind Billy the Kid’s legend.

structure_format.narrative_style: First-person, historical narrative with editorial commentary; part memoir, part report
structure_format.organization: Chronological account of Billy the Kid's life, from his early years to his death, interspersed with anecdotes and observations

key_concepts_lessons: History is shaped by who tells the story, blending fact and myth.
Frontier justice was highly personal, influenced by local loyalties and rivalries.
Outlaw legends often grow beyond the real individuals at their center.
Social and economic instability in the West fostered both criminality and hero worship.
Self-presentation (by Billy the Kid and Pat Garrett) deeply affects historical memory.
style_tone: Defensive (in Garrett's efforts to justify his actions)
Period-specific language reflective of the late 19th century
notable_features: Primary firsthand source about Billy the Kid
Written by the man who killed Billy the Kid
Key document in shaping the legend of both outlaw and lawman
Considered part factual account, part self-justification
cultural_historical_context: Published in 1882, soon after Billy the Kid’s death, as both a response to rampant speculation and public fascination and an attempt by Pat Garrett to establish his own legacy. The book is one of the foundational documents in the mythologizing of the American West, offering insight into how history, media, and personal interests converge to create national legends.
reception_impact: Long considered a crucial source on Billy the Kid, though its accuracy is debated
Influential in popular culture depictions of the outlaw
Generated controversy over its self-serving tone and potential embellishments
Formed the basis of many subsequent books, films, and scholarly debates
comparable_titles: Wyatt Earp: Frontier Marshal by Stuart N. Lake
The Authentic Life of Jesse James by Frank Triplett
Doc Holliday: The Life and Legend by Gary L. Roberts
